case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the SEC may impose civil penalties for securities fraud through in-house administrative adjudication without a jury and consistent with Article II limits on for-cause removal protections for the officials who decide those cases.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. art. III (judicial power), U.S. Const. amend. VII (right to jury trial in “Suits at common law”), U.S. Const. art. II (Executive power/Take Care Clause as applied to removal of executive officers), and the statutory framework authorizing SEC administrative enforcement and adjudication (including the Securities Exchange Act’s administrative proceeding provisions and the APA’s ALJ protections, 5 U.S.C. § 7521).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The SEC (supported by amici such as Public Citizen, NASAA, administrative-law scholars, and NTEU) argues that Congress permissibly assigned securities-law enforcement to an expert agency using administrative adjudication; that SEC civil-penalty proceedings involve “public rights” or otherwise fall within long-accepted administrative adjudication traditions; that requiring a jury trial would disrupt modern regulatory enforcement; and that ALJ tenure protections are constitutionally permissible because ALJs are adjudicators with constrained authority and their protections preserve decisional independence without impermissibly stripping the President of control over core executive functions.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Jarkesy and Patriot28 (supported by amici such as Americans for Prosperity Foundation, Washington Legal Foundation, Morris & Dickson, and Anthony Michael Sabino) argue that when the government seeks civil penalties for fraud, it is pursuing a quintessentially common-law claim requiring a Seventh Amendment jury in an Article III court; that letting the SEC choose between federal court (jury) and in-house proceedings (no jury) unconstitutionally evades the jury-trial guarantee; and that the SEC’s adjudicative structure is doubly unconstitutional under Article II because ALJs are insulated by multiple layers of for-cause removal protection, reducing presidential accountability and control over officers exercising significant federal power.
key_precedents: Atlas Roofing Co. v. Occupational Safety & Health Review Comm’n (1977)
Oil States Energy Servs., LLC v. Greene’s Energy Grp., LLC (2018)
Free Enterprise Fund v. Public Co. Accounting Oversight Bd. (2010)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is Atlas Roofing, bolstered by Oil States’s statement that the Seventh Amendment poses no “independent bar” once a matter is validly assigned outside Article III; but that premise is exactly what is disputed here. Under Tull and Granfinanciera, the SEC’s fraud-based claim seeking punitive civil penalties for past conduct is presumptively a “suit at common law,” and Atlas is best read as limited to enforcement of newly created regulatory duties integral to a comprehensive scheme, not an agency’s discretionary choice to avoid a jury for the same liability theory it could press in Article III court. Justice Kagan’s proposed narrowing—requiring Article III jury adjudication for civil-penalty fraud claims while leaving equitable/forward-looking remedies and clearer public-rights matters to agencies—best preserves precedent, avoids unnecessary disruption, and prevents an end-run around the jury right. Consistent with judicial minimalism and institutional legitimacy, I would resolve on the Seventh Amendment/Article III ground and leave the Article II removal question for another day unless it becomes unavoidable.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is her reading of Atlas Roofing and Oil States to mean that once Congress assigns a “public right” to an agency, the Seventh Amendment is no obstacle; but that premise fails under the original public meaning of “Suits at common law” when the Government pursues a claim functionally mirroring common-law fraud and seeks punitive monetary relief. As the Chief Justice notes, the SEC’s discretionary election between an Article III jury forum and an in-house nonjury tribunal makes the “public rights” label do too much work and effectively toggles a constitutional guarantee on or off—something the Constitution does not permit. Granfinanciera and Tull reinforce that substance controls: backward-looking penalties for alleged fraud are legal in nature and historically tried to juries, and Atlas should not be extended beyond enforcement of newly created regulatory duties integral to a scheme. The Article II concerns identified by Justice Gorsuch and the Chief Justice (layered for-cause insulation under Free Enterprise Fund) further underscore why punitive adjudication of this sort belongs in an Article III court.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is Atlas Roofing (as reinforced by Oil States) that, when Congress validly assigns a “public right” to an agency, the Seventh Amendment poses no independent bar. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, that premise is doing the work here: this SEC action seeks civil penalties for past conduct closely tracking common-law fraud, which under Tull and Granfinanciera is a suit at common law requiring a jury on liability, and Atlas is better confined to newly created regulatory obligations integral to an administrative scheme. The SEC’s discretionary choice between an Article III jury forum and an in-house nonjury tribunal makes the “public rights” label an end-run mechanism, effectively switching a constitutional guarantee on or off by enforcement election. Even if Atlas could be read more broadly, the Article II accountability concerns noted by Justice Thomas (and reflected in Free Enterprise Fund) underscore why punitive penalty adjudications should remain in Article III courts.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s “end-run” point—that identical fraud-and-penalty theories can be tried with a jury in Article III or without one in-house—raises a serious fairness concern, but it does not, in my view, overcome Atlas Roofing’s holding that Congress may assign civil-penalty enforcement of federal regulatory duties to agency adjudication as a public-rights matter. Justice Kagan’s proposed line-drawing (jury required for civil-penalty fraud claims, agency adjudication for equitable relief) is pragmatic, but it effectively narrows Atlas by remedy-label rather than by whether the enforcement action is integral to a comprehensive federal scheme, and it risks destabilizing long-settled administrative enforcement across agencies. Granfinanciera and Tull, as Justice Thomas stresses, rightly look to historical analogues and legal remedies, yet they do not displace Atlas where the Government is enforcing public regulatory obligations rather than resolving a private dispute between private parties; Oil States further indicates that once the Article III assignment is valid, the Seventh Amendment poses no independent bar. On Article II, the Free Enterprise Fund concern flagged by several colleagues supports a targeted severance remedy for any impermissible removal protection rather than a constitutional rule that forces these enforcement actions into mandatory jury trials with significant real-world enforcement consequences for ordinary investors.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that Atlas Roofing (and Oil States’ “no independent bar” language) is the toughest obstacle, but those decisions presuppose a valid public-rights assignment; the prior question is whether this kind of fraud-based, backward-looking claim for punitive money can be removed from Article III and a jury at all. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, under Granfinanciera and Tull we look to the historical analogue and the remedy sought, and a civil-penalty fraud action maps onto a traditional suit at common law for legal relief, making the Seventh Amendment jury right hard to displace by labeling. Sotomayor’s “comprehensive regulatory scheme” framing is not enough where the SEC can toggle the jury right on and off through forum selection, creating the end-run problem Roberts and Justice Barrett highlight and stretching Atlas beyond its comfort zone. I therefore remain with the narrow, workable line: agencies may adjudicate equitable/forward-looking relief, but civil-penalty fraud claims must proceed in Article III with a jury.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Atlas Roofing and Oil States is the most serious counter, but those cases presuppose a valid assignment to a non-Article III/public-rights forum; they do not answer whether Congress may reroute a traditional fraud-and-penalty action—seeking punitive money for past conduct—away from Article III and a jury. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, under Granfinanciera and Tull the Seventh Amendment turns on the historical analogue and the legal nature of the remedy, and the SEC’s discretionary option to proceed either in federal court (with a jury) or in-house (without one) cannot be the lever that switches a constitutional guarantee on or off. Even accepting some administrative civil-penalty adjudications in a comprehensive scheme, Atlas is best confined to genuinely new regulatory-duty enforcement not tracking common-law fraud, and extending it here would allow an end-run around the jury right by relabeling. Justice Thomas’s Article II point about multilayer for-cause insulation reinforces the structural concern, though I would resolve this case primarily on the Seventh Amendment/Article III ground.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to press Atlas Roofing and Oil States, but as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, those cases assume a valid public-rights assignment and are best confined to enforcement of newly created regulatory duties integral to a scheme—not punitive, backward-looking fraud-and-penalty actions that closely track common-law causes and remedies. Under Tull and Granfinanciera, the historical analogue and the legal nature of civil penalties strongly point to a “suit at common law” requiring a jury on liability, and the SEC’s discretionary forum choice makes the Seventh Amendment right too easy to circumvent in practice. Justice Kagan’s proposed narrower line—jury/Article III for civil-penalty fraud claims while leaving room for equitable or forward-looking agency remedies—fits our precedents and protects institutional legitimacy without destabilizing administrative adjudication wholesale. The Article II layered for-cause insulation concerns flagged by Justice Thomas and the Chief reinforce the need for an Article III forum when the agency wields coercive punitive power, though I agree with the Chief that the cleanest disposition here rests on the Seventh Amendment/Article III ground.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point remains Atlas Roofing and Oil States, but I read Atlas as limited to agency enforcement of newly created regulatory obligations that lack a close common-law analogue; this SEC action targets fraud-like misconduct and seeks punitive civil penalties, a quintessentially legal remedy that, under Tull and Granfinanciera, triggers the Seventh Amendment. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the SEC’s discretionary choice between Article III court (with a jury) and in-house adjudication (without one) underscores that Congress has not identified a distinct “public right” but is instead permitting an end-run around a constitutional guarantee. Oil States’s statement that the Seventh Amendment poses no independent bar presupposes a valid public-rights/Article III assignment; under Stern and Granfinanciera, Congress cannot transform a traditional, money-penalty action closely tracking common-law fraud into a public right merely by embedding it in a regulatory scheme. The Article II removal-layer concerns noted by Justice Thomas and others reinforce the structural stakes, but they are not necessary to my vote because the Seventh Amendment/Article III problem is sufficient.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point remains Atlas Roofing and her reading of Oil States that the Seventh Amendment poses no “independent bar” once Congress validly assigns a matter outside Article III, and I take seriously her pragmatic concern about weakening SEC enforcement. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, the threshold problem is whether this fraud-plus-civil-penalty claim—backward-looking, punitive, and historically analogous to common-law fraud under Tull and Granfinanciera—can be assigned to a nonjury, non-Article III forum at all; Oil States assumes a valid assignment rather than supplying it. Atlas Roofing, in my view, is most defensible when tied to enforcement that is integral to a newly created regulatory scheme, not when the Government can toggle constitutional procedure on and off through discretionary forum selection for the same punitive monetary claim. Even if the Article II issues flagged by Roberts and others could be severed, the practical fairness concern of two procedural tracks for identical penalties reinforces that the jury-trial/Article III protection should control here.

John Roberts.reasoning: When the Government seeks civil penalties for alleged fraud, the action closely resembles a traditional suit at common law, and under Tull v. United States and Granfinanciera, S.A. v. Nordberg the Seventh Amendment presumptively requires a jury for the liability determination absent a valid public-rights assignment. Atlas Roofing upheld agency-imposed civil penalties for newly created regulatory duties, but the securities-fraud claim here tracks common-law fraud and the SEC’s discretionary choice of an in-house forum risks allowing the agency to evade the jury-trial guarantee in a way that undermines institutional legitimacy. Separately, the APA’s ALJ protections in 5 U.S.C. § 7521, combined with additional for-cause constraints within the SEC, create the kind of multi-layer insulation rejected in Free Enterprise Fund v. PCAOB, raising serious Article II accountability concerns; the narrowest course is to require Article III adjudication with a jury for these penalty actions rather than invalidate the administrative regime wholesale.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Seventh Amendment preserves the jury-trial right in “Suits at common law,” and an SEC action seeking civil penalties for alleged fraud closely tracks the kind of punitive, money-demanding common-law action that must be tried to a jury, see U.S. Const. amend. VII; Tull v. United States (1987); Granfinanciera, S.A. v. Nordberg (1989). Congress may not evade that constitutional guarantee by routing such a claim into an in-house forum lacking a jury and Article III tenure protections, particularly where the defendant has not consented to the agency adjudication, cf. Granfinanciera; Stern v. Marshall (2011). Separately, insulating SEC ALJs through multiple layers of for-cause removal under 5 U.S.C. § 7521 and Commission oversight impairs the President’s Article II duty to “take Care” that the laws be faithfully executed, as in Free Enterprise Fund v. PCAOB (2010) and Seila Law LLC v. CFPB (2020). Under the Constitution’s original meaning and structure, the SEC cannot both seek civil penalties in an Article I tribunal without a jury and do so through officers insulated from presidential control by dual for-cause protections.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: When the SEC seeks civil penalties for securities fraud, it is pursuing a legal remedy akin to a traditional action at common law, triggering the Seventh Amendment jury-trial right as in Tull v. United States and Granfinanciera, S.A. v. Nordberg; labeling the matter a “public right” cannot by itself eliminate the jury where the Government is effectively prosecuting a fraud-and-penalty claim. Allowing the Commission to route the same claim either to an Article III court (with a jury) or to an in-house tribunal (without one) creates a practical end-run around the Seventh Amendment and undermines Article III’s allocation of the judicial power. Separately, the SEC’s adjudicative scheme raises serious Article II concerns because ALJs are protected by multiple layers of for-cause removal (5 U.S.C. § 7521 plus Commission insulation), the kind of double-insulation this Court found incompatible with presidential control in Free Enterprise Fund v. PCAOB and reinforced in Seila Law and Collins. The practical consequences of such insulation—diminished accountability for officials imposing punitive sanctions—counsel in favor of requiring adjudication in Article III courts with juries for penalty actions.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Congress may assign enforcement of newly created federal regulatory obligations—including the imposition of civil penalties for their violation—to an expert agency through administrative adjudication without triggering a Seventh Amendment jury right when the matter is properly treated as involving “public rights.” Atlas Roofing Co. v. Occupational Safety & Health Review Comm’n (1977) squarely upheld agency adjudication of civil penalties, and Oil States (2018) explains that when a claim is permissibly assigned to a non-Article III forum, “the Seventh Amendment poses no independent bar” to nonjury factfinding. Even Granfinanciera (1989) recognizes that Congress can create closely analogous statutory causes of action and place their adjudication in nonjury forums in appropriate public-rights settings, and federal securities-fraud enforcement is a core federal regulatory scheme. On Article II, the ALJ protections in 5 U.S.C. § 7521 serve decisional independence for adjudicators whose authority is constrained and reviewable within the Commission, and any removal concern can be addressed with a tailored remedy rather than dismantling an enforcement system that protects investors and market integrity.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: When the SEC seeks civil penalties for securities fraud, it is pursuing a classic “suit at common law” in substance—money sanctions imposed for past misconduct—triggering the Seventh Amendment jury right under Granfinanciera and Tull, absent a truly “public-rights” adjudicative scheme. Atlas Roofing allows agency adjudication for statutorily created public-rights enforcement, but Granfinanciera and Stern caution that Congress cannot evade Article III and the jury-trial guarantee merely by labeling a claim regulatory where it mirrors traditional legal actions and imposes punitive monetary relief. Separately, the SEC’s use of ALJs protected by layered for-cause removal restrictions raises a serious Article II problem under Free Enterprise Fund and Seila Law because it unduly insulates officials exercising significant executive power from presidential control, and 5 U.S.C. § 7521’s structure intensifies that insulation in this context. A workable, coherent middle-ground is to require jury-trial adjudication of civil-penalty fraud claims in Article III courts while leaving room for agency adjudication of equitable, forward-looking remedies and other matters more squarely within the public-rights tradition.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: When the government seeks civil penalties for alleged fraud, it is pursuing a claim historically analogous to an action at law, and the Seventh Amendment preserves the jury-trial right as it existed in 1791. Under Granfinanciera and Tull, the nature of the claim and the legal remedy (money penalties) place this within “Suits at common law,” and the SEC cannot evade that constitutional guarantee by routing the case to an in-house forum rather than an Article III court. Nor does labeling the matter “public rights” suffice where the action resembles a traditional common-law fraud/penalty suit rather than a benefits-or-franchise adjudication of the sort discussed in Atlas Roofing and Oil States. Separately, layering for-cause removal protections for SEC ALJs under 5 U.S.C. § 7521 raises the same Article II accountability concern identified in Free Enterprise Fund and reaffirmed in Seila Law, by insulating officials exercising significant federal power from presidential supervision.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: When the SEC seeks civil penalties for alleged fraud—an action historically analogous to common-law suits for monetary relief—the Seventh Amendment generally requires a jury trial in an Article III court, as reflected in Tull v. United States and Granfinanciera, S.A. v. Nordberg. Atlas Roofing upheld agency adjudication for new statutory obligations and penalties in a traditional public-rights setting, but it does not comfortably extend to fraud-based penalty actions that mirror private-rights claims and are brought at the government’s election in a nonjury forum. Separately, the SEC’s ALJ regime raises serious Article II concerns under Free Enterprise Fund v. PCAOB because 5 U.S.C. § 7521’s for-cause protection, combined with layered for-cause constraints on those who supervise ALJs, risks impermissibly insulating officers who exercise significant federal power from presidential oversight. Respecting history, precedent, and the practical need for clear lines of accountability, the constitutional path is for civil-penalty fraud claims to proceed in Article III court with a jury unless Congress has validly created a true public-rights scheme.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: When the SEC seeks civil penalties for alleged fraud, it is pursuing a remedy traditionally obtained in courts of law, triggering the Seventh Amendment right to a jury in a “Suit[] at common law.” See Tull v. United States and Granfinanciera, S.A. v. Nordberg; the action is not transformed into a “public right” merely because Congress created a statutory cause of action, and Atlas Roofing is best read to cover regulatory schemes involving newly created obligations not functionally identical to common-law fraud. Article III reinforces that conclusion because assigning the adjudication of such quintessentially legal claims for money penalties to an in-house tribunal risks withdrawing the judicial power from Article III courts beyond the narrow “public rights” exception. Separately, the APA’s ALJ protections, 5 U.S.C. § 7521, combined with layered for-cause constraints implicated in Free Enterprise Fund v. PCAOB, raise serious Article II concerns when the decisionmaker exercises substantial executive power in imposing penalties.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: When the Government seeks civil penalties for alleged fraud, the action closely tracks a traditional common-law claim for punitive monetary relief, and under Granfinanciera and Tull that trigger indicates the Seventh Amendment jury right applies notwithstanding Congress’s regulatory labeling. Atlas Roofing’s public-rights rationale cannot be read to allow the agency to bypass a jury where the enforcement resembles a classic private-rights fraud action and the SEC can alternatively proceed in Article III court; that prosecutorial forum choice creates an avoidable disparity in procedural fairness. Separately, insulating the adjudicators who find liability and impose penalties through multilayer for-cause removal protections raises serious Article II accountability concerns under Free Enterprise Fund and Seila Law, given the significant coercive power exercised in these proceedings. In light of these structural and fairness problems, I would affirm the respondent’s constitutional objections and require an Article III jury trial for civil-penalty fraud claims.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the SEC may impose civil penalties through in-house adjudication before an administrative law judge without violating the Constitution’s jury-trial right and separation-of-powers limits on insulating adjudicators from presidential control.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. art. II (Executive power/Take Care Clause; presidential removal authority) and U.S. Const. amend. VII (right to jury trial in “Suits at common law”); also implicated are statutory “for-cause” removal protections for SEC ALJs under the Administrative Procedure Act (5 U.S.C. § 7521) and related civil-service/merit-systems removal layers.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The SEC (supported by amici such as Public Citizen, NASAA, administrative-law scholars, and NTEU) argues that Congress may assign certain enforcement matters to administrative adjudication as part of a valid regulatory scheme and that SEC administrative proceedings fit within the public-rights framework such that the Seventh Amendment does not require a jury; further, the ALJ tenure/removal structure is constitutionally permissible (or at least severable/curable) because ALJs function as adjudicators with significant decisional independence, their decisions are subject to agency (Commission) review, and existing removal protections do not impermissibly prevent the President from ensuring faithful execution of the laws.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Jarkesy and Patriot28 (supported by amici such as Americans for Prosperity Foundation, Washington Legal Foundation, Morris & Dickson, and Anthony Michael Sabino) contend that when the SEC seeks civil penalties for fraud-like violations—historically analogous to common-law actions—the Seventh Amendment entitles respondents to a jury in an Article III court; they also argue that SEC ALJs are unconstitutionally insulated from presidential control by multiple layers of “for-cause” protection (Commissioners removable for cause, ALJs removable only for cause by the Merit Systems Protection Board, whose members also have for-cause protection), violating Article II under the rule against multi-level tenure insulation and rendering the administrative forum unconstitutional for penalty actions.
key_precedents: Atlas Roofing Co. v. Occupational Safety & Health Review Commission (1977)
Oil States Energy Services, LLC v. Greene’s Energy Group, LLC (2018)
Free Enterprise Fund v. Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (2010)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is Atlas Roofing, reinforced by Oil States’ statement that the Seventh Amendment is not an “independent bar” once Congress properly assigns a matter to a non-Article III tribunal; I take that seriously. But as Justice Kagan emphasizes, that formulation assumes the antecedent—whether this kind of coercive civil-penalty action for fraud-like conduct is a “public right” that may be withdrawn from an Article III court and a jury—and Granfinanciera and Tull counsel that Congress cannot evade the jury guarantee by rerouting a historically legal, punitive-money claim into an agency forum. Atlas Roofing is therefore best read narrowly as approving administrative penalties in settings involving newly created public obligations integrated into a regulatory scheme, not as a license to adjudicate traditional fraud-analog penalties without a jury whenever the Government enforces a statute. Consistent with my minimalist approach and institutional concerns, I would decide only the Seventh Amendment issue here and leave the Article II removal questions for another day.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that Atlas Roofing upheld agency assessment of civil penalties and Oil States repeats that, given a valid non-Article III assignment, the Seventh Amendment is not an “independent bar.” But that formulation assumes the crucial premise—whether this fraud-analog, punitive-money claim is the sort of “public right” that can be withdrawn from Article III in the first place—and Granfinanciera and Tull (as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize) treat such coercive monetary liability as a paradigmatic “Suit at common law” requiring a jury under the original public meaning. Read textually and historically, Congress cannot extinguish the jury right by relabeling a traditionally legal claim as regulatory enforcement and routing it to an agency; Atlas Roofing is best confined to genuinely new statutory duties not mirroring common-law causes with punitive monetary relief. Justice Alito and Justice Gorsuch’s Article II concerns further underscore how far this in-house scheme departs from the Constitution’s structural safeguards, reinforcing the case for not extending Atlas Roofing beyond its proper historical bounds.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is Atlas Roofing, coupled with Oil States’ statement that the Seventh Amendment is no “independent bar” once Congress has validly assigned a matter to a non-Article III tribunal. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, that framing assumes the decisive antecedent: whether this kind of fraud-analog, punitive civil-penalty action is properly withdrawable from Article III and the jury right at all, which Tull and Granfinanciera treat as the core of a “Suit at common law.” Atlas Roofing is therefore best confined to its setting (administrative enforcement of newly created statutory obligations in an integrated scheme) and cannot be read to let Congress extinguish the jury guarantee simply by choosing an agency forum for what is functionally a traditional legal claim for coercive money. Oil States does not expand public-rights doctrine to swallow that limitation; it presupposes a valid non-Article III assignment and, in context, concerns a distinct public-franchise reconsideration rather than the Government’s pursuit of punitive money for fraud-like conduct.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan press the hardest point that Tull and Granfinanciera treat punitive civil penalties as legal relief and warn against Congress evading the jury right by relabeling a private-rights claim as “public.” But Atlas Roofing is not just a relabeling case; it upheld agency adjudication of civil penalties as part of an integrated federal enforcement scheme, and Oil States underscores that once a matter is properly assigned outside Article III, the Seventh Amendment does not independently reimpose a jury requirement—so the decisive question is the public-rights fit, not the fraud analogy alone. Here the Government is enforcing a modern regulatory program to protect market integrity (and, pragmatically, the investors least able to absorb systemic fraud), and I am not convinced the Constitution freezes Congress into 18th-century procedural forms whenever money is at stake in public enforcement. Justice Thomas’s originalist framing is serious, but under my methodology I would treat any structural overreach (including Article II layering) with targeted severability/remedial tailoring rather than constitutionalizing a broad jury-trial rule that would substantially weaken effective public enforcement.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s Atlas Roofing/Oil States point is the best case for the SEC, but it hinges on the antecedent that this enforcement action is a properly reassigned “public right.” As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Granfinanciera and Tull treat punitive, coercive money—especially for fraud-analog conduct—as the core of “Suits at common law,” and Congress cannot avoid the jury guarantee merely by channeling that classic legal claim into an agency forum. Oil States’ statement that the Seventh Amendment is not an “independent bar” presupposes a valid non‑Article III assignment; it doesn’t answer whether this penalty-for-fraud claim is eligible for such assignment in the first place, and Atlas Roofing is best confined to integrated regulatory duties not so closely tracking common-law fraud. Consistent with my pragmatic textualism, the narrow, workable resolution is to require an Article III jury trial for these SEC civil-penalty fraud actions and leave the Article II removal issues for another day.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s invocation of Atlas Roofing and Oil States is the best argument for the SEC, but those decisions do not, on an original public-meaning account of the Seventh Amendment, permit Congress to re-route into an agency a claim that is substantively a traditional action at law for punitive money against a private party. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Oil States’ “no independent Seventh Amendment bar” language presupposes a valid non-Article III assignment; the antecedent question is whether this is a public right at all, and Tull/Granfinanciera treat civil penalties and fraud-analog liability as the heartland of “Suits at common law.” Atlas Roofing is best read as addressing administrative enforcement of newly created regulatory duties in a setting not so closely tracking common-law fraud and punitive monetary relief, and it cannot be extended to let Congress evade the jury right by forum designation. Even if one tried to push Atlas Roofing further, Justice Thomas’s Article II layering concern underscores the structural anomaly of this in-house scheme and counsels against enlarging non-Article III adjudication here.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point remains Atlas Roofing, reinforced by Oil States’ statement that the Seventh Amendment is no “independent bar” when Congress validly assigns adjudication to a non-Article III tribunal. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, that proposition assumes the key antecedent—whether this kind of fraud-analog civil-penalty action is properly treated as a public right—and Granfinanciera and Tull caution that Congress cannot evade the jury guarantee by routing a traditionally legal, punitive monetary claim into an agency. Atlas Roofing is most plausibly confined to administrative enforcement of newly created regulatory duties in an integrated scheme, whereas here the nature of the claim and remedy tracks the common-law core of “Suits at common law.” Consistent with an institutional, precedent-respecting approach, I would resolve on the narrow Seventh Amendment ground and avoid the broader Article II removal issue unless necessary.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to press Atlas Roofing and Oil States, but those cases only relax the Seventh Amendment once we are within a category Congress may constitutionally assign to non-Article III adjudication; they do not answer the antecedent question whether this penalty-for-fraud action is a “Suit[] at common law.” As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Tull and Granfinanciera treat punitive civil penalties and fraud-analog claims as paradigmatically legal, and the original public meaning of the Seventh Amendment does not permit Congress to extinguish the jury right by redescribing such a claim as regulatory enforcement. Oil States’ narrow, franchise-based setting (patent validity) does not support extending “public rights” to core monetary-liability adjudications between the Government and a private party. Accordingly, Atlas Roofing is best confined to its “new statutory obligations” context, and I would hold the Seventh Amendment requires an Article III jury forum here without reaching the Article II removal issue.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that Atlas Roofing upheld agency-imposed civil penalties in a modern regulatory scheme and that Oil States suggests the Seventh Amendment is not an “independent bar” once Congress validly assigns a matter to a non-Article III tribunal. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, that framing assumes the key premise—whether this kind of fraud-analog, punitive-money claim can be withdrawn from Article III and a jury in the first place—and Granfinanciera/Tull cut hard against treating it as a mere “public right” simply because the Government is the plaintiff. Procedurally and practically, letting the SEC unilaterally choose an in-house forum for coercive penalties that look like traditional legal relief risks the very unfairness the Seventh Amendment’s jury guarantee is meant to check, and Atlas Roofing’s “new statutory obligation” rationale seems ill-fitted where the remedy and claim track common-law fraud. I therefore remain with Respondent on the narrow Seventh Amendment disposition, without reaching the Article II removal issues unless necessary.

John Roberts.reasoning: When the SEC seeks civil penalties for fraud-like violations, the action is closely analogous to a traditional suit at common law for money penalties, bringing it within the Seventh Amendment’s jury-trial guarantee as described in Tull v. United States and Granfinanciera, S.A. v. Nordberg. Although Atlas Roofing upheld agency adjudication of civil penalties for “new statutory obligations” under a public-rights framework, this case sits nearer the line where Congress may not withdraw from Article III courts and juries claims that replicate core common-law liability. On the Article II question, the SEC’s ALJ removal structure risks the multi-layer insulation condemned in Free Enterprise Fund v. PCAOB, and a narrow ruling requiring jury trials for SEC civil-penalty actions would protect constitutional structure while minimizing disruption by leaving other administrative adjudications and prospective severability questions for another day. Given institutional legitimacy and precedent, the least disruptive course is to hold only that the Constitution requires an Article III jury trial when the SEC seeks civil penalties of this kind.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Seventh Amendment preserves the jury-trial right in “Suits at common law,” and an SEC action seeking civil penalties for fraud-like conduct is historically analogous to legal claims traditionally tried to a jury; under Tull v. United States and Granfinanciera, S.A. v. Nordberg, Congress may not avoid that constitutional guarantee by routing such claims to an in-house tribunal under the “public rights” label. Separately, Article II vests the Executive power in the President, and insulating SEC ALJs through multiple layers of for-cause removal protection (5 U.S.C. § 7521 plus Merit Systems protections atop commissioners’ tenure) impermissibly diminishes presidential control contrary to Free Enterprise Fund v. PCAOB and Seila Law. Because these constitutional defects go to structure, I would not extend deference to precedent that departs from the Constitution’s original meaning, and the SEC must pursue penalties in an Article III court with a jury available. The in-house adjudication scheme, at least as applied to civil penalties here, violates both the Seventh Amendment and separation of powers.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: When the SEC seeks civil penalties for fraud-like violations, it is pursuing a coercive monetary remedy historically characteristic of “Suits at common law,” triggering the Seventh Amendment jury-trial right under Tull v. United States and Granfinanciera, S.A. v. Nordberg; that Congress authorizes an administrative forum cannot by itself extinguish that right where the claim is not a quintessential “public right.” In addition, the ALJ removal scheme—ALJs removable only for cause under 5 U.S.C. § 7521, layered beneath for-cause protection for Merit Systems Protection Board members and SEC Commissioners—creates the kind of multi-level insulation from presidential control condemned in Free Enterprise Fund v. PCAOB and is difficult to reconcile with Article II’s Take Care duty. Whatever the virtues of efficient agency enforcement, practical consequences cannot override the Constitution’s structural protections and the jury guarantee when the government chooses to demand penalties. The appropriate course is to require penalty actions of this kind to proceed in Article III courts with juries (or, at minimum, invalidate the insulation to restore presidential accountability).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Congress may assign enforcement of new statutory obligations, including the imposition of civil penalties, to administrative adjudication as part of a comprehensive regulatory scheme without triggering a Seventh Amendment jury requirement, so long as the matter fits within the “public rights” framework. Atlas Roofing Co. v. Occupational Safety & Health Review Comm’n, 430 U.S. 442, 450 (1977), squarely upheld agency adjudication of civil penalties for violations of a federal statute, and Oil States Energy Servs., LLC v. Greene’s Energy Grp., LLC, 138 S. Ct. 1365, 1379 (2018), reiterates that where Congress properly assigns a matter to a non-Article III tribunal, the Seventh Amendment poses no independent bar to nonjury factfinding. On the Article II challenge, any concern under Free Enterprise Fund v. PCAOB, 561 U.S. 477 (2010), about multiple layers of for-cause protection can be addressed through severability or tailored relief rather than dismantling the SEC’s adjudicatory forum wholesale, preserving access to effective enforcement that protects investors and market integrity. Given the practical consequences for vulnerable investors and the functioning of federal regulatory enforcement, I would uphold the SEC’s use of ALJ proceedings for civil penalties while permitting a narrow constitutional fix if needed under 5 U.S.C. § 7521.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: When the SEC seeks civil penalties for securities-fraud violations against a private party, the action is functionally a “Suit[] at common law” within the Seventh Amendment’s core, and the public-rights label cannot do all the work to convert a jury-triable legal claim into agency adjudication. Granfinanciera instructs that Congress may not evade the jury right merely by routing a traditionally legal, coercive monetary remedy to a non-Article III forum; Tull likewise underscores that civil penalties are the kind of legal relief that ordinarily triggers a jury entitlement. Atlas Roofing and Oil States recognize room for administrative enforcement in genuine public-rights schemes, but this penalty-for-fraud posture looks too close to the traditional model of government seeking punitive money in court to treat the jury right as optional. Given that conclusion, I would not reach the deeper Article II issue about layered “for-cause” removal protections under 5 U.S.C. § 7521, though Free Enterprise Fund/Seila Law would make the structure difficult to defend if it were necessary to decide.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: When the SEC seeks civil penalties for fraud-like conduct from a private party, it is pursuing a claim historically analogous to an action at law, so the Seventh Amendment preserves the right to a jury in an Article III court rather than an agency tribunal. Granfinanciera and Tull instruct that Congress cannot evade the jury-trial guarantee by relabeling a traditional legal claim as regulatory enforcement, and Atlas Roofing’s public-rights rationale does not extend to adjudicating core private-rights liability for penalties in-house. Separately, SEC ALJs’ tenure protections—removal only for cause under 5 U.S.C. § 7521, layered atop for-cause protection for the officials who can remove them—raise the same Article II problem identified in Free Enterprise Fund by unduly restricting the President’s ability to ensure faithful execution. The Constitution’s plain allocation of judicial power and the President’s Take Care responsibility thus forbids this combination of penalty adjudication without a jury and multi-layer insulation from presidential control.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: When the SEC seeks civil penalties for fraud-like conduct, the action is closely analogous to traditional common-law claims for money damages, and the Seventh Amendment protects a jury-trial right in such “Suits at common law,” see Tull v. United States and Granfinanciera, S.A. v. Nordberg. Atlas Roofing upheld agency assessment of civil penalties for newly created regulatory duties within a public-rights framework, but its logic is harder to extend to classic fraud analogues where the Government is effectively pursuing a punitive money remedy against a private party. Separately, the SEC ALJ removal regime (5 U.S.C. § 7521 combined with MSPB/Commission protections) raises serious Article II concerns under Free Enterprise Fund and Seila Law by layering for-cause protections that impede presidential accountability; at minimum, that structure underscores why these penalty actions should proceed in Article III courts with juries rather than insulated in-house adjudication.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: When the SEC seeks civil penalties for securities fraud, it pursues a coercive monetary remedy historically characteristic of “Suits at common law,” triggering the Seventh Amendment jury-trial right absent a valid “public rights” assignment; Granfinanciera, S.A. v. Nordberg, 492 U.S. 33 (1989), and Tull v. United States (1987) instruct that legal claims for money resembling common-law actions ordinarily require a jury, and Congress cannot avoid that requirement merely by routing the claim to an agency tribunal. Even if some administrative adjudication is permissible under Atlas Roofing Co. v. OSHRC (1977), this penalty action is closer to the fraud-like, private-rights paradigm than to a specialized regulatory liability newly created and integrated into a public-rights scheme. Independently, the layered “for-cause” removal protections for SEC ALJs under 5 U.S.C. § 7521, combined with additional for-cause insulation for the reviewing/removal actors, raise the Article II problem identified in Free Enterprise Fund v. PCAOB (2010) by unduly restricting the President’s ability to ensure faithful execution. Given the constitutional avoidance and structural concerns, the SEC may not impose these civil penalties through in-house ALJ adjudication in this posture without a jury and without an Article II-compliant removal structure.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Congress may, consistent with Article III and the Seventh Amendment, assign enforcement of newly created statutory obligations—along with civil penalties for their violation—to administrative adjudication as part of a comprehensive regulatory scheme, as this Court upheld in Atlas Roofing Co. v. OSHRC and reaffirmed through the public-rights framework referenced in Oil States. Even where a statutory cause of action bears some resemblance to common-law fraud, Granfinanciera recognizes that Congress can place such matters outside the Seventh Amendment’s jury requirement when it properly commits their resolution to a non-Article III tribunal. On the Article II issue, while multilayer “for-cause” removal protections raise concerns under Free Enterprise Fund, the SEC’s review authority over ALJ decisions and the availability of severance as a remedy (rather than invalidating the forum wholesale) counsel upholding the adjudicatory scheme, especially given practical consequences for fair, uniform enforcement. Accordingly, I would vote to sustain the SEC’s ability to proceed in-house and, if necessary, treat any removal defect in 5 U.S.C. § 7521 and related layers as curable through severance rather than a basis to require juries for all penalty actions.
